Every Tuesday, the clockmaker found an extra minute in his shop.

It appeared at closing time: sixty small silver seconds rattling in the drawer where he kept spare springs. He tried returning them to the town clock, but by morning they were back.

So he began giving them away.

He gave one to a woman who had missed her train, and she used it to call her father. He gave one to a boy who had broken a window, and the boy used it to tell the truth before anyone asked. He gave one to a baker, who stood in his empty kitchen and ate a warm roll without doing anything else.

Years passed. The clockmaker grew old, and still the minutes came.

On his last Tuesday, he opened the drawer and found it empty. He waited, listening to the clocks around him tick out their different versions of the hour.

Then someone knocked.

It was the baker, older now too, holding a paper bag. Inside were two warm rolls.

“I thought you might have a minute,” he said.
